source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/AitBentaleb_2023_NeuroimagingMetaAnalysis.pdf, all 15 pages: the unnumbered Taylor & Francis cover page plus printed pp. 211-224, read in full (text, Tables 1-3 and the figure captions; the reference list was skimmed, and the online supplement, S1-S4, was not available to me). Printed pp. 214 and 216 (Table 1, the Results text and Table 3 with its footnote) were re-checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi. Every number quoted below was read off the printed page.

claims.overstatement: One point of precision rather than an overstatement of substance. '33 functional-imaging studies in 628 healthy volunteers' is the review's own total (p. 219) and my sum of Tables 1 and 2 reproduces it (198 + 59 + 371 = 628), but the two clusters the claim then reports do not rest on those 628 people: the resting-state cluster comes from 10 studies and 257 participants and the executive-function cluster from 9 studies and 138 participants, which is the 395 the review itself names as 'yielding results'. The other 233 participants are in the 14 task studies of other cognitive domains, which produced nothing, so attaching 628 to the findings makes the base sound about 60% larger than it is. A second small thing: 'no decrease was found in any analysis' is stated outright by the review only for the across-domain task analysis (p. 214); for the resting-state and executive-function analyses it is an inference from the fact that only increases are reported and Table 3 has no decrease rows, which is sound because the method imputes maps of both increases and decreases (p. 213), but it is an inference.
claims.note: Every number the claim takes from this source is exact, checked on the rendered Table 3 (p. 216): resting state, left anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri BA 24, MNI 0; 30; 20, Z = 4.265, p < 0.001, 658 voxels, 495 after TFCE correction; right insula BA 47, 36; 24; -6, Z = 3.432, p < 0.001, 30 voxels; right fusiform gyrus BA 30, 22; -34; -16, Z = 2.933, p < 0.002, 26 voxels; executive-function tasks, right Heschl's gyrus BA 48, 44; -16; 6, Z = 3.306, p < 0.001, 160 voxels, 142 after correction; right anterior cingulate BA 10, 6; 52; 8, Z = 2.889, p < 0.002, 26 voxels. The claim's use of 495 rather than the 496 printed in the Results text (p. 214) is the right choice, since 495 is the table's own footnote. The counts also check: 33 studies retained, 10 resting-state (8 fMRI, 2 PET) and 23 task-based, 9 of them executive-function studies; the search arithmetic (876 + 11, minus 808, 79 screened, 46 excluded, 33 retained) is internally consistent. 'Glucose use, blood flow or the fMRI signal' is right for the pooled literature: Table 1 holds one PET glucose study, PET and ASL blood-flow studies, BOLD and fALFF. 'No effect size or interval is recoverable from a coordinate-based meta-analysis' is correct; the review reports Z-values, voxel counts and thresholds only. The claim keeps this to acute administration in healthy volunteers, which is what the review included.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (meta-analysis results of ketamine-induced brain activations) with its footnote
anchors.extracted: Resting-state studies, ketamine > placebo: left anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri BA 24 (MNI 0; 30; 20), Z = 4.265, p < 0.001, 658 voxels, marked as the only resting cluster to remain significant after TFCE correction, at 495 voxels, with a cluster breakdown spanning left and right anterior cingulate, left median cingulate and right median cingulum; right insula BA 47 (36; 24; -6), Z = 3.432, p < 0.001, 30 voxels; right fusiform gyrus BA 30 (22; -34; -16), Z = 2.933, p < 0.002, 26 voxels. Executive-function tasks, ketamine > control condition: right Heschl's gyrus BA 48 (44; -16; 6), Z = 3.306, p < 0.001, 160 voxels, remaining significant after correction at 142 voxels, breakdown right insula and right Heschl's gyrus; right anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri BA 10 (6; 52; 8), Z = 2.889, p < 0.002, 26 voxels. Every row is an increase; the table contains no decrease.

anchors.locator: Results › Meta-analysis of task-related activity, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Across cognitive domains (all 23 task-based studies), the meta-analysis revealed no significant cluster of increased or decreased activation during acute ketamine administration relative to placebo. Only when the analysis was restricted to the executive-function domain did clusters of increased activation appear.

anchors.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (resting-state studies) and Table 2 (task-based studies, p. 215)
anchors.extracted: 33 articles retained: 10 resting-state (8 fMRI, 2 PET) and 23 task-activation (22 fMRI, 1 PET). Resting-state studies: 198 participants in the ketamine columns plus 59 in the comparison groups of the three between-group studies (Table 1 TOTAL row), 75% male by the table's study-level average, mean age 27.71; three used racemic, two S-ketamine, five unspecified; eight of ten assessed psychotomimetic symptoms. Task studies: 371 participants, 72% male, mean age 27.4; 12 racemic, 7 S-ketamine, 4 unspecified. The commonest task domains were executive functions and verbal fluency (9 studies), episodic memory (4) and negative emotions (3). My sum of the three participant figures gives the review's stated total of 628.

The review names its own sample size as a limitation: n = 628 in all, of which n = 395 are in the two analyses that produced results, which limited the power to detect differences and to run task-specific analyses. Of the 19 studies in those two analyses, only 8 reported a plasma ketamine concentration (mean 98.08 ng/mL, printed with a dispersion of 37.68, range 16.6 to 183), and the review calls the variation and absence of plasma information a limitation. Recomputation: the 9 executive-function studies hold 138 participants and the 10 resting-state studies 257 including comparison groups, which is the 395.

anchors.locator: Methods › Coordinate-based meta-analysis and › Meta-analytic procedure
anchors.extracted: Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images (SDM-PSI 6.11) pooling the peak coordinates and t-values reported in the original papers, imputing effect-size maps of increased and decreased activations; maps built at an uncorrected voxel threshold of z > 2.5 with cluster extent above 20 voxels, with family-wise correction by threshold-free cluster enhancement (1000 permutations, corrected p < .05). Connectivity studies and studies using a restricted set of a priori regions of interest were excluded by design. No appraisal of the risk of bias of the included studies is described anywhere in the Methods.

key_findings.correction: Right as far as the article goes, with one nuance worth carrying: the review states that no cluster of increased or decreased activation was significant only for the across-domain task analysis (p. 214). For the resting-state and executive-function analyses it reports increases and says nothing about decreases, so 'no decrease reached significance in any of the three analyses' is an inference from Table 3 and from the Methods, where the method is said to impute maps of both increases and decreases (p. 213). The inference is sound; the wording should show that it is one.

Study-size ranges and both totals check out. Adding the per-analysis bases would help a claim writer: the 10 resting-state studies hold 257 participants (198 plus the 59 comparison-group participants) and the 9 executive-function studies 138, which together make the review's 395.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: 496 in the Results text on p. 214, 495 in the Table 3 footnote on p. 216, both read on rendered pages.

I recomputed from the same eight values (16.6, 75, 75, 75, 100, 110, 150, 183) and got mean 98.075, sample SD 51.11, population SD 47.81, against the printed 37.68. I also checked that no set of eight values with that mean and containing both 16.6 and 183 can have an SD of 37.68, since those two values alone contribute more squared deviation than 37.68 allows, so the printed dispersion is wrong rather than drawn from a different set of studies.
Confirmed by recomputation: 198 + 59 + 371 = 628, and the figure appears only in the Limitations on p. 219 while the Results on p. 214 give 198 and 371.

The mixing of bases is real but is a step more tangled than the note says. Table 1's mean age of 27.71 is reproduced only by weighting across all 257 resting-state participants including the comparison groups; weighting across the 198 the text names gives 27.61, and the unweighted study-level mean is 27.45. The male share of 0.75 is the unweighted mean of the ten study-level proportions; weighted across the 198 it is 0.69 and across all 257 it is 0.66 (the card's figure). Table 2's row is consistent either way (0.72 weighted and unweighted; mean age 27.4 is the weighted value, the unweighted being 27.8). So the correction should read: Table 1's age is participant-weighted over 257, its sex figure is study-level, and the two are not on the same base.
Confirmed on the rendered p. 214: the column is headed 'm/f ratio' and carries 1 for the all-male samples, which only works as a proportion of men.

Confirmed on the rendered p. 216: Figure 1's legend reads that the figure displays the brain regions that were impaired at rest by ketamine relative to the placebo or baseline condition, and adds that the threshold was lowered to obtain better graphic results. Every result in Table 3 is an increase in activation.

Confirmed: the Methods list ketamine type among the resting-state moderators and do not name dose (p. 213), while the Results report dose (bolus and infusion) and do not report ketamine type (p. 214).
Confirmed: TFCE in the abstract and Methods, TCFE in the Discussion and in the Table 3 footnote on the rendered p. 216.
Confirmed: selection criteria run (i), (ii), (iii), (iiii), (iv), (v), (vi) and the extraction list runs (i) to (x) then (xiv), (xv) (pp. 212-213).
Confirmed: heterogeneity is given only as a range across all significant clusters (0.15% to 6.45%) and publication bias only as all p-values above 0.24 (p. 214), with no per-cluster values.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is the right instrument and critically low is the right overall rating: three of the critical items (protocol, appraisal of the included studies, and risk of bias carried into the interpretation) are 'no', and any one of them would be enough. The item-level judgments match what the article shows, including the documented extension for item 7, recorded as no information because the list of the 46 excluded full texts is in a supplement I could not see either; per METHODS 5.3 the overall rating should therefore be marked provisional, and I did not see that marking. Two item readings I would keep as they are but note: item 5 (selection in duplicate) is a 'yes' on the strength of one sentence saying two authors reviewed the studies and decided by consensus, and item 15 is a 'yes' for Egger's tests that were run on 9 and 10 studies, which is below the number at which those tests mean much, as the card's own reporting issue 9 says.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. The clearest instance is the distance between the Results and the Conclusions: five clusters, two of them surviving correction, become 'ketamine disrupts the salience network at rest' and 'ketamine activates task-irrelevant regions during executive functions while preventing the de-activation of the task-negative DMN' (p. 219), although no deactivation contrast was analysed and the rostral anterior cingulate cluster on which the default-mode reading rests did not survive correction. The authors do caution twice in the Discussion (pp. 218, 219) that the small uncorrected clusters must not be over-interpreted, which the Conclusions then do not carry.

missed: Possible overlapping samples inside the executive-function analysis, which is the one that produced the Heschl's gyrus cluster. In Table 2, Daumann et al. (2008) and Daumann et al. (2010) share every printed characteristic (n = 14, mean age 32.1, sex ratio 0.57, S-ketamine, executive functions), and Nagels et al. (2011) and Nagels et al. (2018) likewise (n = 15, mean age 27, sex ratio 1, S-ketamine); Honey et al. appear three times across the table. The review never says whether these are independent samples, and SDM-PSI assumes they are. If either pair is one dataset analysed twice, the 9 studies and 138 participants behind the corrected task cluster are fewer than they look, and METHODS 6.3 would not count such pairs as independent replication. This is worth a line on the card and a caution in any claim that cites the number of studies.

The literature was searched in September 2021 (p. 212) and the article carries a 2024 print year, so the evidence base is about two and a half years older than the citation suggests. The card records the search date in the recruitment field but does not name the gap as a currency limit, and a claim dated 2024 should say when the search closed.

Three of the ten resting-state studies had no placebo condition and three compared separate groups rather than the same people (Table 1, columns Placebo and Design), so the pooled 'ketamine > placebo' resting contrast mixes within-person placebo differences, within-person baseline differences and between-group differences. The card's comparison field records the design split accurately, but the key findings and the can_establish line present the resting-state result as a single contrast; the moderator test for control condition was null in 10 studies, which cannot settle it.
